universalAnswers.whatHappened: California issued Executive Order N-9-26 on September 18.
universalAnswers.plainLanguageIdentity: A government instruction that speeds existing oversight work and requests recommendations on possible additional laws.
universalAnswers.evidenceBasis: Signed executive order, official announcement and EFF advocacy response.
universalAnswers.evidenceLimits: The November recommendations do not yet exist, and no supplied source proves a universal shutoff design would work.
universalAnswers.readerRelevance: The headline sounds immediate; the operative text separates current implementation from future proposals.
universalAnswers.affectedPeople: California agencies and, if later proposals become law, large frontier-model developers and people affected by their systems.
universalAnswers.changesNow: Agencies have new deadlines and a November recommendation assignment.
universalAnswers.uncertainty: Technical feasibility, efficacy, legal design and later adoption remain open.
universalAnswers.readerAction: Check the operative verb and its deadline before treating a policy headline as a current requirement.
universalAnswers.betterQuestion: Which parts are already required, which are being implemented, and which are still recommendations?

legal-policy.legalStatus: An effective executive order directing state-agency implementation work and recommendations; the listed possible statutory amendments are not enacted requirements.
legal-policy.jurisdiction: California state agencies are directly bound by the order; later proposals could affect large frontier developers covered by future California law.
legal-policy.parties: Governor Gavin Newsom issued the order; the Government Operations Agency and Governor’s Office of Emergency Services carry the directed work; large frontier developers are possible subjects of later amendments.
legal-policy.allegationVsFinding: The operative directions and dates are established by the signed order. The Governor’s “kill switch” label is announcement framing; technical feasibility and efficacy remain for recommendation.
legal-policy.currentEffect: Agencies must accelerate existing oversight implementation and submit recommendations. No universal company shutoff requirement takes effect from this order.
legal-policy.unresolvedQuestions: Technical feasibility, efficacy, statutory text, scope, enforcement design and later adoption remain unresolved.
legal-policy.nextMilestone: November 16, 2026 recommendations; then the distinct May 1, 2027 and December 1, 2027 implementation deadlines.

translation.newsVersionExact: California’s September 18 executive order took effect immediately, but it did not install a universal AI shutoff or order every company to build one.
translation.actualMeaningExact: The “kill switch” is one idea the order tells state agencies to study for possible changes to existing law.
translation.mechanismExact: By then, the agency and California’s emergency-services office must recommend whether proposed legal amendments are technically feasible and potentially effective.
translation.familiarExampleExact: “Recommend by November 16” describes a policy-development step; it does not mean “companies must install this now.”
